implementation_notes: Default in Spring applications: the ApplicationContext is the hub, publishEvent(Object) wraps non-ApplicationEvent payloads, and @EventListener methods (optionally @Async, @Order, or @TransactionalEventListener for after-commit delivery) are the subscribers. Nothing registers explicitly, which is why the wiring is discovered rather than read; the docs stress that publication is only a hand-off.
pitfalls: Listeners run on the publishing thread unless @Async is used, so they must not block or do I/O.
@TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT) is required when the reaction must not fire for a rolled-back transaction.

variants.name: JDK Flow/SubmissionPublisher (stdlib, backpressured)
variants.implementation_notes: Standard-library realization with flow control: SubmissionPublisher is a Flow.Publisher that delivers to each subscriber through the supplied Executor with an independent bounded buffer, subscribers request items through Flow.Subscription, and submit() blocks while offer() reports or drops when a subscriber is saturated. Prefer it for high-rate fan-out where backpressure and monitoring (estimateMinimumDemand, estimateMaximumLag, getNumberOfSubscribers) matter more than Spring's annotation convenience.
pitfalls: Delivery is asynchronous, so ordering across subscribers is only per-subscriber and tests must await or drain the buffer.
A subscriber that throws from onNext is cancelled - failing subscribers must handle their own errors.
close()/closeExceptionally() must be called, otherwise item generators relying on onComplete never finish.

variants.name: Guava EventBus (legacy standalone bus)
variants.implementation_notes: The classic library bus: register(Object) scans the instance for @Subscribe methods (single-argument, type-routed including assignable supertypes), post routes the event to all of them, and unhandled events are republished as DeadEvent; AsyncEventBus dispatches through an Executor. Guava's own javadoc now recommends against new use (poor discoverability, reflection under optimizers, no backpressure), so treat it as a legacy-compatible choice.
variants.code_sketch:
EventBus bus = new EventBus("domain");   // or AsyncEventBus(executor)

bus.register(this);        // methods annotated @Subscribe receive matching event types
bus.post(new OrderPlaced(id, total));
bus.unregister(this);      // EventBus keeps strong references
pitfalls: Subscribers run in sequence on the posting thread and subscriber exceptions are caught and logged rather than propagated, so failures are easy to miss.
Registering an object that is never unregistered keeps it alive and keeps receiving events.
Reflection-based registration breaks under R8/ProGuard-style shrinking unless the subscriber methods are kept.
